blocks.text: Imagine a world where some questions can never be answered by any computer program. This is the realm of decidability in computability theory.

blocks.markdown: In computability theory, we explore the boundaries of what problems can be solved by algorithms. A key concept here is **decidability**. This lesson will introduce you to decision problems, the distinction between decidable and undecidable languages, and the role of a decider.

blocks.title: Decidability
blocks.text: A decision problem is said to be decidable if there exists an algorithm that can determine the answer (yes or no) for every input in a finite amount of time.

blocks.markdown: To formalize this, consider a decision problem as a language $L$ over some alphabet $\Sigma$. A decision problem is decidable if there exists a Turing machine that halts on every input and correctly decides whether the input belongs to $L$.

blocks.title: Example of a Decidable Problem
blocks.prompt: Consider the problem of determining if a given string is a palindrome.

steps.text: Define the language $L = \{ w \mid w \text{ is a palindrome} \}$. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards.
Construct a Turing machine that reads the input string from both ends towards the center, checking for equality at each step.
If all corresponding characters match, the machine accepts the string; otherwise, it rejects.

blocks.answer: This problem is decidable because the Turing machine halts and correctly decides for every input whether it is a palindrome.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's contrast this with an undecidable problem. An undecidable problem is one for which no algorithm can determine the answer for all possible inputs.

blocks.title: Example of an Undecidable Problem
blocks.prompt: Consider the Halting Problem: given a description of a Turing machine and an input, determine whether the machine halts on that input.

steps.text: Assume there exists a decider for the Halting Problem. This decider, $H$, takes a Turing machine $M$ and input $w$ and returns 'yes' if $M$ halts on $w$, 'no' otherwise.
Construct a new machine $D$ that uses $H$ to decide if $M$ halts on $w$, and if so, enters an infinite loop.
If $H$ says $M$ halts, $D$ loops forever. If $H$ says $M$ doesn't halt, $D$ halts. This leads to a contradiction, proving no such decider $H$ can exist.

blocks.answer: The Halting Problem is undecidable because assuming a decider leads to a logical contradiction.

blocks.title: Decider vs Recogniser
blocks.text: A decider is a Turing machine that halts on every input, deciding membership in a language. A recogniser may not halt on some inputs but will accept if the input is in the language.

blocks.markdown: In summary, decidability is a fundamental concept in computability theory, distinguishing problems that can be algorithmically solved from those that cannot. Understanding the difference between deciders and recognisers is crucial in this context.

points: A problem is decidable if there exists a Turing machine that halts on all inputs and correctly decides membership.
The Halting Problem is a classic example of an undecidable problem.
A decider halts on every input, while a recogniser may not.
